known_from: ch02-term-registry.json (terms defined there count as known in every chapter)

terms.definition: one of the categories a classifier chooses between, e.g. "virginica" or "not virginica". Careful: Python also says "class" for a blueprint objects are made from (each Scikit-Learn model type is one); this chapter uses both, and the sentence always shows which.
a model that predicts a class (a category) rather than a number.
a small, famous table of 150 flowers: 4 measurements per flower (petal and sepal length and width, in cm) plus the flower's species. It ships inside Scikit-Learn.
the coloured leaf-like parts of a flower. The iris data measures each flower's petal length and width in centimetres.
the kind of iris a flower is: setosa, versicolor or virginica.
the line where the model's answer changes from one class to the other.
the width of the empty band (the "street") between the decision boundary and the nearest training rows on each side.
the book's picture of the margin: the boundary is the centre line, the margin is the street's width, and the training rows should stay off the street.
choosing the boundary with the widest possible street, not just any line that separates the classes.
to work well on new rows the model has never seen, not only on its training rows.
a training row that sits on the edge of the street (or on it, or on the wrong side). Only these rows decide where the boundary goes.
insisting that every training row stays off the street and on its correct side, with no exceptions.
allowing some rows onto the street (or even across it), in exchange for a wider street.
a training row that lands on the street or on the wrong side of the boundary.
two classes that one straight line (or flat plane) can separate completely.
the SVM setting that sets how strict the street is: a small C allows many rows on the street (wider street, more regularization); a large C allows few (narrower street, less regularization).
Scikit-Learn's fast SVM classifier for a straight-line boundary.

the score an SVM computes for a row before it decides: positive means the positive class, negative the other, and the size says how far from the boundary the row sits. At the street's edges it is exactly +1 or −1.
a distance with a plus or minus sign attached; the sign says which side of the boundary the row is on.
a number from 0 to 1 (0% to 100%) for how likely something is.
a model for classification (despite its name) that outputs a probability for each class; the book's Chapter 4 covers it.
Scikit-Learn's general SVM classifier: slower than LinearSVC, but it supports kernels.
said of probabilities that can be taken at face value: among rows given 80%, about 80% really are that class.
classification with only two classes, e.g. virginica or not.
extra columns made from the existing ones by squaring, cubing and multiplying them together (x1², x1·x2, x2³, ...).
the highest power used when making polynomial features: degree 3 goes up to cubes like x1³ and x1²·x2.
a made-up two-feature dataset from Scikit-Learn's `make_moons()`: two interlocking crescent shapes, one per class, with some random scatter (noise).
a way to get exactly the model you would get by adding many extra features, without ever building those features. b09 shows why it works.
an SVM kernel that behaves as if polynomial features up to a chosen degree had been added.
a setting of the polynomial kernel: how much the high-degree terms count compared with the low-degree ones.
the number of combinations growing so fast that it quickly becomes unmanageable.
a chosen reference point; each row gets a new feature saying how similar it is to that point.
a formula that turns "how far is this row from that point" into a score, highest when they coincide.
the setting of the Gaussian RBF (and other kernels) that sets how quickly similarity falls off with distance: large gamma = a narrow bell, each row's influence stays close to it.
two free programming libraries written in C: LinearSVC runs on liblinear, SVC on libsvm.
how the training time grows as the data grows. "O(m × n)" reads "roughly proportional to m times n", where m is the number of rows and n the number of features.
Scikit-Learn's classifier trained by stochastic gradient descent; with the right settings it behaves like a linear SVM.
training by many small steps, each one nudging the model's numbers to lower the error on one small batch of rows ("stochastic" = the batches are picked at random).
a small group of rows used for one training step.
training on data too big for memory, by reading and learning from it one chunk at a time.
mostly zeros: a sparse row has only a few non-zero values.
using the SVM street for regression: fit as many rows as possible INSIDE a street of fixed width, and predict the centre line. LinearSVR and SVR are the Scikit-Learn classes.
the SVM-regression setting that fixes the street's half-width: rows closer than epsilon to the prediction count as no error at all.
an SVM-regression property: rows already inside the street have no effect at all on the fitted model.
w: one number per feature that the model multiplies each feature by before adding them up.
b: one extra number added after the weighted sum. It shifts the boundary without tilting it. (In later chapters "bias" also names a kind of error; here it is only this number.)
what training is told to make as small (or as large) as possible.
a condition every answer must satisfy, written after "subject to" in an optimization problem.
a function is differentiable where it has a clear slope (its derivative); solvers follow the slope downhill.
ζ (zeta), one per training row: how far that row is allowed onto the street or past it.
a standard kind of optimization problem (a squared objective with straight-line constraints) that off-the-shelf solvers can solve exactly.
bowl-shaped: the function has a single lowest point, so going downhill always reaches it.
the SVM's error for one row: 0 when the row is on its correct side and off the street, growing in a straight line the further it strays.
the error score training adds up over the rows and tries to make small.
the training problem written in terms of w and b (one number per feature, plus one).
the same training problem rewritten with one number α (alpha) per training row; it touches the rows only through dot products between pairs of rows.
multiply two rows column by column and add the results: (3, 2)·(1, 4) = 3×1 + 2×4 = 11.
the little ᵀ in wᵀx: it turns a column of numbers into a row, so wᵀx is just the dot product of w and x.
φ(x): the transformation that turns a row into its bigger version with extra features, e.g. (x1, x2) → (x1², √2·x1·x2, x2²).
a mathematics result: if a kernel K meets a few conditions (such as K(a, b) = K(b, a)), a matching transformation φ is guaranteed to exist.
a kernel built from an S-shaped curve; rarely useful.
having infinitely many columns; the Gaussian RBF's φ turns each row into such a vector, which is why it can never be built.
the strength setting of several regularized models from the book's Chapter 4: a bigger alpha means MORE regularization, the opposite direction to C.
(alpha) the number the dual problem learns for each training row: 0 for most rows, positive only for the support vectors. Not the same thing as the regularization setting alpha.
two regularized versions of linear regression from the book's Chapter 4; their strength setting is also called alpha.
updating a trained model with new rows without retraining it from scratch.
turning a problem with several classes into several yes/no problems ("this class, or not?"), one model each, and picking the most confident.
a small table in Scikit-Learn: chemical measurements of 178 wines from 3 growers.
